faq.q: Why are the buttons greyed out?
faq.a: Your role is viewer or public, and changes need an admin key. Mint one on the host with `nemo-console mint-key admin` (it prints the path of a 0600 key file, never the key), then paste the key with the key button in the top bar. The key is kept in this tab's sessionStorage only.

faq.q: What is the difference between off, down and unknown?
faq.a: `off` is an opt-in system that is stopped on purpose (Dynamo, the OpenShell gateway): normal. `down` is a system that should answer and does not. `unknown` means the console's own status check failed, usually because a path is wrong; look for the problem `console.repo_root.missing` and set `NEMO_CONSOLE_REPO_ROOT`.

faq.q: Does the console run the Fix command of a problem for me?
faq.a: No. Each problem shows one exact command with a Copy button; you run it in a terminal (from the repo root unless it says otherwise). Actions that the console does run are on the Actions or Lifecycle tab, and each asks you to confirm.

faq.q: Why do some actions ask me to confirm?
faq.a: Every action has a danger level. Safe ones run at once; disruptive ones (they interrupt a running service or spend router tokens) and destructive ones (state is lost) open a dialog that states the exact effect. Config applies and rollbacks always ask too.

faq.q: What do the Form view and the Edit checks on a Config tab do?
faq.a:
TOML and YAML files open as a form: one control per value, typed (a number field takes only numbers, true/false is a switch, fixed choices are a list). A form edit rewrites only that value in the file, so comments and layout stay; the Text view and the diff show exactly what changed.

Edit checks update as you type: syntax errors with their line, the rules of AIPerf profiles, Model Optimizer recipes, Evaluator suites and Switchyard routes, and secret-looking values the console would refuse to save. They are early warnings. The server's own validator still decides: Check (or Ctrl+S) runs it, and Apply always runs it first.

faq.q: What does the (i) button next to a setting do?
faq.a: It opens a short description of that setting: what it is, what changing it does, the values it accepts and when a change takes effect (or why the file is read-only here). Esc or a click outside closes it. Sections the console knows have an About this section button too. The descriptions are the console's own (`i18n/fields.en.json`); for a Dynamo command-line flag the pop-up also shows that flag's entry from the Params tab. A key the console has no description for still shows its type, accepted values and its comment from the file.

faq.q: Where can I see what was changed, and by whom?
faq.a: The Audit page lists every mutating call with the key that made it. Parameters are redacted; chat text and file bodies are never stored. It needs an admin key.

faq.q: The charts are empty after a restart. Is something broken?
faq.a: Usually not. The 15 minute history lives in memory and starts empty; the 1 h and 24 h windows come from rollups written once a minute. Wait a minute, or pick the 15 min window. A system that is not serving has no numbers to chart.

faq.q: A page says "Something went wrong" right after an upgrade.
faq.a: If the message mentions a module that "does not provide an export", the browser mixed old and new console files. Reload once with Ctrl+Shift+R. Since 0.3.1 every frontend file is revalidated on each load, so this does not recur.

faq.q: Where do I change URLs, the poll interval or the playground credential?
faq.a: On the Settings page. URL changes need a console restart. Credentials are stored as the NAME of an environment variable, never the value; the variable must be set in the console's own environment (for example `~/.config/nemo-console/env`).

overview.lead: The Overview is the console's front page: a map of how requests flow from the agent clients through the gateway and router to the engines, and one card per system with its health, version, components and problems. It refreshes every 5 seconds and changes nothing.

steps.title: Sign in
steps.body: Every page except the health check needs a key. On the first start the console writes an admin key to `bootstrap-admin.key` in its state directory; paste it with the key button in the top bar, or mint another on the host. The key stays in this tab only, so each new tab asks again.

steps.title: Read the topology
steps.body: The topology card draws the path a request can take. Its edges are built from each system's health plus a few probes, so they show a plausible path, not observed traffic. Engines come from the `topology_engines` setting: one that is stopped on purpose is drawn off, a missing container off (not deployed).

steps.title: Scan the system cards
steps.body: Each card shows the system's health, version, a one-line summary, its components and its problems. Start with anything down, then degraded. Every problem carries one exact fix command with a Copy button.

steps.title: Open a system
steps.body: The system's name or its Open button leads to its own page: status, config, actions and playground, and its own Getting started and FAQ tabs.

faq.q: Is the topology live traffic?
faq.a: No. It is drawn from health checks and probes (router liveness, the engine containers you list), so it shows where a request could go. To see where requests actually went, open Switchyard's Routing tab or the trace boards of your observability stack.

faq.q: The topology shows an engine I never run.
faq.a: The engine nodes come from the `topology_engines` setting, whose default lists the author's engines. Set `NEMO_CONSOLE_TOPOLOGY_ENGINES` for your deployment and restart the console. A container that does not exist is drawn off (not deployed), not as a fault.

faq.q: Every system looks absent and the paths look wrong.
faq.a: The console cannot find the systems' directories. Look for the problem `console.repo_root.missing` and set `NEMO_CONSOLE_REPO_ROOT` to the checkout that holds them, then restart the console.

faq.q: A card says "version unknown".
faq.a: The system did not report a version, usually because it is not answering (check its health) or because that system does not expose one.

faq.q: Can I start or stop systems from here?
faq.a: No. The Overview only reads. Actions, config edits and test requests live on each system's page, and each one asks you to confirm.

faq.q: Does a screen reader hear when something changes?
faq.a: Yes. When a system's health changes between two refreshes, the console announces it in a live region.

audit.lead: The Audit log is the append-only record of every change made through the console: when, which key, which system, which action or file, the parameters (redacted) and the HTTP status. Chat text and file bodies are never stored. Only admins can read it.

steps.title: Sign in with an admin key
steps.body: A viewer key sees "Admin only". Mint an admin key on the host and paste it with the key button in the top bar.

steps.title: Pick a system
steps.body: The Log tab shows the newest 200 calls. The filter narrows them to one system; Refresh reloads.

steps.title: Read a row
steps.body: When (UTC), the actor (the key's id) and its role, the system, the action or file, the redacted parameters and the HTTP status: green for success, red for 400 and above.

steps.title: Keep a copy
steps.body: The log lives in `console.db` in the console's state directory. To back it up while the console runs, use SQLite's backup command, and treat the copy as sensitive: the database also holds key hashes and the stored config revisions.

faq.q: Which calls are recorded?
faq.a: Authenticated, authorised calls that change something: applies, rollbacks, actions, settings saves, playground requests. Reads are not recorded.

faq.q: Why is a refused request missing from the log?
faq.a: Denied requests (401, 403, 421, 429) never reach the audit table. They are counted in `nemo_console_denied_requests_total` on the console's `/metrics`, kept in a 100-entry memory ring, and summarised in the console log at most once a minute.

faq.q: Are secrets or my prompts in the log?
faq.a: No. Parameters are redacted, chat text and file contents are never stored, and credentials are only ever referenced by the name of their environment variable.

faq.q: Can I see more than 200 rows?
faq.a: The page asks for 200. The API returns up to 500 at a time.

faq.q: Can I edit or delete entries?
faq.a: Not through the console: the log is append-only. It is an ordinary SQLite table on the host, so anyone with access to the state directory can still change the file; protect that directory (it is created 0700).

faq.q: Who is the actor?
faq.a: The id of the key that made the call, with its role. The console has one user; give each tool or person its own key if you want to tell them apart.

settings.lead: Settings has three parts: how this browser shows the console (theme), the key this tab uses (session), and the console backend's own settings (system URLs, the poll interval and the names of the environment variables that hold the playground credentials).

steps.title: Pick a theme
steps.body: Dark, light or follow the system. The choice is kept in this browser.

steps.title: Set the key for this tab
steps.body: Paste a bearer key and Save. It is kept in this tab's sessionStorage only, never in localStorage, and Clear forgets it. The line under it shows your role and the trust mode.

steps.title: Check the system URLs
steps.body: Backend settings lists the URL the console uses for each system. They must be loopback addresses; anything else is refused. A saved change takes effect only after the console restarts.

steps.title: Name the playground credentials
steps.body: Each playground uses a credential held in an environment variable of the console process. Enter the variable's NAME, not its value; the status next to it says `[set, N chars]` or `[unset]`. Allowed names are `LITELLM_*`, `NEMO_CONSOLE_PLAYGROUND_*` and `*_API_KEY`.

steps.title: Restart to apply
steps.body: After saving URLs, restart the console so they take effect.

faq.q: I saved a URL and nothing changed.
faq.a: URL changes need a console restart; the page says so after a save. Restart with `nemo-console stop` and `nemo-console open`.

faq.q: A credential shows `[unset]`.
faq.a: The named variable is not in the console process's environment. Add it to `~/.config/nemo-console/env` (keep the file 0600) or the unit's environment, then restart the console.

faq.q: Saving was refused with `invalid_setting`.
faq.a: Credential fields take an environment variable NAME from the allowed families (`LITELLM_*`, `NEMO_CONSOLE_PLAYGROUND_*`, `*_API_KEY`), never a value. Use a name in one of those families.

faq.q: Why are the fields greyed out?
faq.a: Your key has the viewer role. Viewers can read the settings; saving needs an admin key.

faq.q: Where do I change container names, paths or the repo root?
faq.a: Those are environment-only settings (`NEMO_CONSOLE_*`, for example `NEMO_CONSOLE_REPO_ROOT`), listed in section 2 of the operations guide. Set them in the env file and restart; this page does not edit them.

faq.q: Why does every new tab ask for the key again?
faq.a: The key lives in each tab's sessionStorage, so it never reaches disk through the browser. That is deliberate.

faq.q: What does the trust line mean?
faq.a: `bearer token` is the default: every call needs a key. `loopback admin` appears only if `NEMO_CONSOLE_TRUST_LOOPBACK=true` was set, which makes ANY local process an admin without a key; the console turns it off by itself when the host is not loopback or `NEMO_CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is set.

switchyard.lead: NeMo Switchyard routes each chat request to a tier (a fast model first, a capable one for hard turns) according to its `routes.toml`. Here you read its traffic, edit its routes with an automatic rollback and send test requests through it.

steps.title: Check that it is running
steps.body: The header above the tabs shows its health. If it reads down with the problem `switchyard.down`, copy the fix shown there (a `docker compose up -d --no-build` in its compose directory) and run it.

steps.title: Read the traffic
steps.body: The Routing tab shows requests, errors and tokens for the chosen window (15 min, 1 h, 24 h), the share by tier, route and model, and the routing decisions as they happen. The numbers come from the last 5,000 routing events.

steps.title: Send a test request
steps.body: The Playground sends one chat request through a route you pick and streams the answer; nothing is stored. It needs an admin key, and the router credential named on the Settings page must be set in the console's environment.

steps.title: Change a route
steps.body: On the Config tab open `routes.toml`, edit it in the Form or the Text view (the Edit checks panel flags unknown targets and clients as you type), then Check: that checks the TOML, the route semantics and runs Switchyard's own dry-run in a throwaway container. Apply shows the diff, takes a backup, writes the file, recreates the container and rolls back by itself if the health check fails.

steps.title: Maintain it
steps.body: The Actions tab can recreate the container, reset the in-memory stats and dry-run the live `routes.toml`.

faq.q: What does "capable tier dark" mean?
faq.a: The capable model of a `stage_router` route maps to an engine container that exists but is not running, so hard turns cannot be served. Switchyard turns degraded and the fix is that engine's start command. Passthrough routes do not count. A running but broken engine is only noticed with the opt-in probe `NEMO_CONSOLE_CAPABLE_PROBE=true`, which sends one 1-token completion per capable alias at most every 5 minutes (real, billed router requests).

faq.q: Why are the "served by" badges in the Playground empty?
faq.a: The console looks for served-by headers whose names are guessed. Real Switchyard responses do not send them, so empty badges are normal, not an error.

faq.q: Check says "dry-run could not start (image ... missing?)".
faq.a: The dry-run uses the Switchyard image with `--pull never`, and the image is not on this machine. Start the service once (or build or load the image), then validate again.

faq.q: Apply failed with "the file changed since you loaded it" (409).
faq.a: Someone, or an earlier apply, changed `routes.toml` after you opened it. Reload from disk, merge your edit again and re-apply. The write is compare-and-swap, so nothing was overwritten.

faq.q: Why is my `base_url` rejected?
faq.a: Route targets must be loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`) or a bare in-network service name without dots, and must not contain `user:pass@`. Point the route at a local engine or a service on the Docker network.

faq.q: What does `switchyard.config.drift` mean?
faq.a: `routes.toml` on disk differs from the routes the running server loaded. Recreate the container (Actions, Recreate Switchyard) to load the file.

faq.q: Why did the counters drop to zero?
faq.a: Reset stats zeroes the in-memory counters behind `/v1/stats`, and every apply or recreate restarts the server, which resets them too. The routing log (`routing.jsonl`) is not touched, so the Routing tab keeps its history.

faq.q: The Playground answers 401.
faq.a: The router credential is wrong or missing. On the Settings page check which environment variable the Switchyard playground uses (default `LITELLM_API_KEY`) and that it holds a valid key in the console's environment.

relay.lead: NeMo Relay is the agent gateway: it forwards agent traffic to the router under a plugin policy and records ATOF events and ATIF trajectories. It runs as a systemd user unit (default `nemo-relay-gateway.service`). Here you read its health, policy findings and trace counts, edit its routes and run diagnostics.

steps.title: Check the gateway
steps.body: The Status tab shows the plugin attestation, the unit and gateway state, and how many ATOF files and ATIF trajectories exist. Any answer under 500 from the gateway's `/health` counts as up; a 404 is expected.

steps.title: Bring it back if it is down
steps.body: With `relay.gateway.down`, restart the unit. Diagnostics, Restart gateway does the same and waits for several healthy checks and a stable process id.

steps.title: Read the policy findings
steps.body: Problems such as a weak attestation, exporters off or PII redaction off come from `plugins.toml`. They are human decisions: the console reports them and never changes them.

steps.title: Edit the routes
steps.body: On the Config tab only `routes.toml` is editable. Its validator is non-authoritative (a mirror of Relay's schema), so the gateway restart after apply is the real check. `plugins.toml` and `config.toml` are shown read-only.

steps.title: Run diagnostics
steps.body: Diagnostics runs Gateway status, Doctor (offline), List agents and Validate plugins. Passing doctor or validate does not prove the gateway starts; the restart does.

faq.q: Why can't I edit `plugins.toml` or `config.toml`?
faq.a: They hold the signature-enforcement policy. A web console that could loosen it would be the easiest way around it, so both are read-only by design (an apply answers 403 `read_only`). Edit them by hand and restart the gateway.

faq.q: What does `relay.config.newer_than_gateway` mean?
faq.a: `plugins.toml` changed after the gateway started, so the running gateway still uses the old policy. Restart the gateway.

faq.q: The gateway is up but shows `relay.gateway.upstream_error`.
faq.a: The router behind it does not answer `/health/liveliness`, so requests through the gateway will fail. Fix the router first. The console never polls `/v1/models` through the gateway, because the router would log every keyless call as an error.

faq.q: What does `relay.atof.large` mean?
faq.a: The ATOF directory is over 1 GiB. Relay has no retention of its own; prune rotated files by hand.

faq.q: Why is there no Playground tab?
faq.a: It appears only when the backend offers a playground for Relay. It sends the key named for Relay on the Settings page (default `LITELLM_API_KEY`), because the gateway's `/v1/*` answers 401 without a bearer.

faq.q: A problem says `binary 'nemo-relay' not found on PATH`.
faq.a: The console searches `PATH` plus `NEMO_CONSOLE_EXTRA_BIN_DIRS` (default `~/.local/bin`). Add the directory that holds `nemo-relay` to that setting and restart the console.

dynamo.lead: NVIDIA Dynamo serves a model through a frontend and a vLLM worker (docker compose), pinned to a GPU. It is opt-in: while it is stopped its health is off, which is normal. The console starts and stops only Dynamo's own containers, after a preflight that names everything else on the card.

steps.title: Look at the state
steps.body: The Status tab shows the frontend and worker containers and, while serving, requests, in-flight requests, TTFT and ITL p95 and KV cache use. "Loading" (degraded) during a cold start is normal; it takes several minutes.

steps.title: Run the preflight
steps.body: On the Lifecycle tab, Preflight is a read-only check of what shares the worker's card and which router aliases go dark while Dynamo holds it. Every up, down and restart runs it first.

steps.title: Start it
steps.body: If the default model holds the card, Up is refused with `dynamo.up.exclusive_engine`: run the fix shown (the `NEMO_CONSOLE_DYNAMO_START` command) from the repo root, which stops the default model in the right order. Otherwise press Up on the Lifecycle tab and confirm.

steps.title: Tune it
steps.body: The Parameters tab is a form for the worker and frontend flags. Preview shows the compose override it would write; apply recreates the worker and rolls back if it does not become healthy.

steps.title: Send a test request
steps.body: The Playground talks to the Dynamo frontend directly, bypassing the router and any output filtering on it.

steps.title: Stop it
steps.body: Down on the Lifecycle tab stops Dynamo's containers only. To give the card back to the default model, run its start command afterwards.

faq.q: Up is refused: "the worker's card is in use by ...".
faq.a: Another container runs on the worker's card (`dynamo.up.card_in_use`). If it is the opt-in 27B engine, run Up again with "stop" ticked: the console stops that one label-verified container. For any other container, identify it with `docker inspect` and stop it with its own tooling; the console never stops the default model.

faq.q: Up refused: "the CPU mocker is running" (or the real worker is).
faq.a: The mocker and the worker serve the same model name and cannot run together. Press Down first. Up mock starts a CPU-only stand-in that needs no VRAM, handy for checking the console without a GPU.

faq.q: Up failed with "timed out".
faq.a: Up waits up to 600 s for the worker to serve, inside the action timeout (default 900 s, `NEMO_CONSOLE_ACTION_TIMEOUT_S`, or a `dynamo.up` entry in `NEMO_CONSOLE_ACTION_TIMEOUTS`). Check the Status tab first: "loading" means it is still starting. Raise the timeout if your model loads slower.

faq.q: Parameters says the live stack runs from another compose file.
faq.a: A repo override file is in use (`dynamo.compose.override`, for example a variant stack). The console override would replace that stack's worker command, so Parameters refuses. Change the variant's compose file in git, or bring it down first.

faq.q: What does `dynamo.compose.untrusted` mean?
faq.a: The running containers' compose label names a file outside the configured compose directory, a missing file or another project, or the containers disagree. Nothing ran and nothing falls back. Take that stack down with the files it was started from, or point `NEMO_CONSOLE_REPO_ROOT` at its checkout.

faq.q: What does `dynamo.card.contended` mean?
faq.a: The worker runs or restarts while an exclusive engine is on one of its cards. They cannot share the VRAM, so the worker will crash-loop. Press Down, or stop the other engine first if you want Dynamo.

faq.q: Why is there no Config tab?
faq.a: The backend exposes the compose file (read-only) and the generated override, but this page offers the Parameters form and Lifecycle instead, so the flags stay inside a checked allowlist.

faq.q: Why do Dynamo events look like log lines?
faq.a: They are redacted container log lines, not an allowlist of metadata fields as for the other systems. Secrets are redacted, but treat them as raw logs.

skillevaluator.lead: NVIDIA SkillEvaluator scores agent skills (folders with a `SKILL.md`) for quality, security and duplication. It is a CLI, not a service: the console runs it on demand and keeps each report in its state directory.

steps.title: Check the launcher
steps.body: The Status tab shows whether `skillevaluator-local` (the lab wrapper) or `skillevaluator` was found on PATH (`~/.local/bin` is searched), its version, whether the router answers, and how many skills exist under `<repo>/.claude/skills/`.

steps.title: Evaluate one skill
steps.body: On the Evaluate tab run Evaluate a skill. `static` makes no model calls; `tier1` adds an LLM judge through the router; `tier1+2` adds embedding deduplication against the other skills.

steps.title: Read the report
steps.body: Show a stored report opens a run (newest first) with the Tier 1 and Tier 2 findings. The verdict is the report's own `overall_status`.

steps.title: Check the whole catalog
steps.body: Static check of every skill runs Tier 1 static checks on each skill, one run each, and prints a score table. About 2 s per skill.

steps.title: Measure the Skill Lift (Tier 3)
steps.body: Tier 3 runs an agent on the skill's eval cases with and without the skill, in a sandboxed runner container, and a judge scores both. It needs the `skillevaluator-local` wrapper and the lab's runner, spends router tokens, runs in the background, one at a time, and takes minutes up to about an hour.

faq.q: Tier 3 says `skillevaluator.live.needs_wrapper`.
faq.a: Tier 3 was asked for with plain `skillevaluator`. Install the lab wrapper with `clients/skillevaluator/install.sh` in the lab repo.

faq.q: A Tier 3 report says "launch: NOT READY: ...".
faq.a: The runner is missing a piece (image, network, broker or egress container). The lab's check names which one.

faq.q: Tier 2 reports `skillevaluator.tier2.no_embeddings`.
faq.a: Tier 2 could not get embeddings through the router. In the lab they come from Ollama: start it, then run Tier 2 again.

faq.q: A second Tier 3 run is refused as busy.
faq.a: One live run at a time (`skillevaluator.live.busy`). Watch the running one in the runs list on the Status tab; Show a stored report with its id shows its progress.

faq.q: A Tier 3 run is `interrupted`.
faq.a: The console stopped or restarted while it ran. Start it again. After a hard kill of the console, check for a leftover job container with `docker ps --filter label=ai-lab.skilleval.job`.

faq.q: I use plain `skillevaluator`, not the wrapper. What does it need?
faq.a: `SKILL_EVAL_LLM_PROVIDER`, `SKILL_EVAL_LLM_BASE_URL`, `SKILL_EVAL_LLM_API_KEY`, `SKILL_EVAL_LLM_MODEL` and, for Tier 2, `SKILL_EVAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL` in the console's environment (a 0600 env file). Tier 3 needs the wrapper either way.

faq.q: How many reports are kept?
faq.a: The newest 200 runs. Each `run.json` holds metadata and redacted error text only; the reports sit next to it in the console state directory.

datadesigner.lead: NVIDIA Data Designer generates synthetic datasets from config scripts through the lab router: validate, preview a few records, then create the full set. It is a CLI the console runs on demand; runs and their reports are kept in the console state directory.

steps.title: Check the launcher
steps.body: The Status tab shows the `data-designer-local` version, whether the router answers, the providers and model aliases from the tool's own config, and any create run in progress. Install it with the lab's `clients/data-designer/install.sh`.

steps.title: Open or write a script
steps.body: The Dataset scripts tab lists the config scripts. A script defines `load_config_builder()`. Check and Apply EXECUTE the script (that is how Data Designer loads it), so read it before you run either.

steps.title: Preview a few records
steps.body: Actions, Preview records runs the script for a small sample and keeps the report and the sample records.

steps.title: Create the dataset
steps.body: Actions, Create a dataset runs in the background, one at a time, for up to an hour, and writes a copy in the format you pick (parquet, csv, jsonl or json) under `~/Datasets`.

steps.title: Review the records
steps.body: The Runs tab shows each run's verdict, record count and destination; open a run for a records table and the list of files in its run directory.

faq.q: Which model generates my records?
faq.a: The model aliases named in the script, resolved through the providers that Show provider config lists. An alias that points at a cloud provider sends your prompts and records there; keep to local aliases for private data.

faq.q: Why does the records table stop at 2,000 rows?
faq.a: The console keeps at most the first 2,000 records of a run (`records.jsonl`) for review. The dataset files in the run directory and the copy under `~/Datasets` always hold the full set.

faq.q: Can I download the dataset from the console?
faq.a: No. The console lists the files of a run but does not serve them; open them on disk (the run detail shows each path).

faq.q: My create run is `interrupted`.
faq.a: The console stopped while it ran. Start Create a dataset again.

faq.q: Check models asks for a script. Why?
faq.a: The CLI checks the models a config uses, so the action takes one of the dataset scripts.

faq.q: How many runs are kept?
faq.a: The newest 100, in the console state directory.

openshell.lead: NVIDIA OpenShell is the sandbox gateway that contains Data Designer runs: limited filesystem access, a default-deny network and credentials held by the gateway. It starts on demand, so a stopped gateway is off, not down.

steps.title: Read the state
steps.body: The Status tab shows the CLI version, the gateway and forwarder containers, whether the CLI is connected, whether the sandbox network `openshell-docker` is internal, and whether any port is exposed.

steps.title: Check the prerequisites
steps.body: Actions, Run doctor validates the local prerequisites for a gateway (Docker reachable). Read-only.

steps.title: Look at the sandboxes
steps.body: List sandboxes, Show a sandbox (phase and active policy), Sandbox logs and Gateway container logs are all read-only. Logs are redacted.

steps.title: Prove the policy
steps.body: Prove sandbox policy checks the policy against the credential descriptor derived from the provider profile (no key is read). Its findings are for a human to review.

steps.title: Start or stop the gateway
steps.body: Start the gateway refuses unless the sandbox network is internal. Stop the gateway refuses while sandboxes exist unless you force it. Delete a sandbox is destructive.

faq.q: Why can't I edit the gateway, policy or provider files?
faq.a: They are trust files. A web console never loosens a sandbox's trust policy, so they are shown read-only by design. Edit them in the lab repo and review the change there.

faq.q: The gateway is off. Is that a fault?
faq.a: No. `data-designer-local` starts it on demand for each run, and Start the gateway starts it by hand. Off is the normal resting state.

faq.q: What does `openshell.version.skew` mean?
faq.a: The CLI and the gateway report different versions. It is information, not a fault; upgrade them together when you next touch the install.

faq.q: The status names a gateway registration. Which one is used?
faq.a: The console always passes `-g openshell`, the lab's registration, because the CLI can also hold other, stale registrations. Register the lab gateway under that name.

faq.q: A sandbox phase shows as "Other".
faq.a: Only `Ready` is a phase name the console knows for sure; any other phase is grouped as Other. Show a sandbox gives its exact phase.

dcgm.lead: GPU telemetry from this host's dcgm-exporter and from every DCGM host the lab's Prometheus scrapes, plus per-GPU diagnostics in a throwaway container. Read-only, except the exporter's field list.

steps.title: Check the exporter
steps.body: The Status tab shows the exporter container and version, whether `/metrics` answers, that `/debug/pprof/` does NOT answer 200, and a table of every DCGM host with its up state.

steps.title: Read the GPUs
steps.body: Further down the Status tab: temperature, power, utilisation and memory per GPU, a trend chart per value for the chosen window, and a collapsed table with every value.

steps.title: Run a diagnostic
steps.body: Diagnostics run in a throwaway container from the full DCGM image, which you pull once yourself (the image named by the `dcgm_diag_image` setting; the console never pulls). Start with Actions, Discover GPUs, then Diagnostic, level 1 on one GPU.

steps.title: Change which fields are collected
steps.body: On the Config tab edit `counters.csv`, Check (a non-authoritative check against the field lists in the exporter image) and Apply. The exporter re-reads the file; tick restart if a field does not show up.

faq.q: What does `dcgm.exporter.vulnerable` mean?
faq.a: The exporter is older than 4.8.3, which is affected by CVE-2026-47483. Upgrade the exporter image.

faq.q: The exporter is not running. How do I start it?
faq.a: In the lab it is part of the observability stack's gpu profile.
faq.cmd: cd observability && docker compose --profile gpu up -d dcgm-exporter

faq.q: Will a diagnostic disturb a running model?
faq.a: It can. Both levels are marked disruptive because they exercise the GPU; level 2 runs longer. Prefer a card that is idle.

faq.q: Is "XID last" a count of errors?
faq.a: No. It is the exporter's LAST XID code. The total is a separate value.

faq.q: What happens when I restart the exporter?
faq.a: `/metrics` is unavailable for about 10 s and the profiling fields take 10 to 20 s to return, so Prometheus shows a short gap.

faq.q: Why is there no version for the other hosts' exporters?
faq.a: Prometheus does not expose it, and the console does not guess. Only this host's exporter version is checked.

aiperf.lead: NVIDIA AIPerf load-tests router models from named presets, one run at a time, and reports TTFT, ITL, latency and throughput from each run.

steps.title: Install the wrapper
steps.body: In the lab, `clients/aiperf/install.sh` then `clients/aiperf/mint-key.sh` put `aiperf-local` on PATH with its own router key file. The Status tab then shows the wrapper, the router, the key file and the presets.

steps.title: Choose a preset
steps.body: The presets live in `profiles.yaml` on the Config tab. Validation is authoritative and there is nothing to restart after an apply.

steps.title: Run a load profile
steps.body: Actions, Run a load profile takes a preset and a model and runs in the background. It is disruptive: it loads a live engine that others may be using. Keep loads small on shared engines.

steps.title: Read the results
steps.body: The Status tab charts TTFT, ITL, latency and throughput of the newest run; Actions, Show a stored run gives the full numbers of any run.

faq.q: A second run is refused.
faq.a: One run at a time. Wait for the running one to finish; its report appears under Show a stored run.

faq.q: My run failed with a 400 from the router.
faq.a: The model name is not one the router serves, or its engine is down. The report carries the router's own message; pick an alias whose engine is up.

faq.q: Does a run download a tokenizer?
faq.a: No. The `builtin` tokenizer is vendored in the lab repo with a pinned checksum and installed by the wrapper before every run.

faq.q: My run is `interrupted`.
faq.a: The console stopped while it ran. Start it again.

faq.q: The numbers look far worse than usual.
faq.a: The engine may be busy with other traffic, or the run hit the AIPerf key's own rate limits on the router. Compare with a quiet moment and a smaller preset before drawing conclusions.

guardrails.lead: A NeMo Guardrails server (input and output self-check rails) in an internal-network container with no internet. Rails configs are editable with validation and rollback; probe checks and a playground go through the rails.

steps.title: Install and start it
steps.body: In the lab run `security/nemo-guardrails/mint-key.sh` and `install.sh`, then start it with `docker compose up -d` in that directory, or with Actions, Start Guardrails.

steps.title: Check the state
steps.body: The Status tab shows the server, gateway and router-broker containers, `/v1/health`, the served configs and the isolation checks. An error appears if the server ever joins a non-internal network or publishes a port.

steps.title: Check the rails
steps.body: Actions, Check the rails sends fixed benign, jailbreak and harmful probes. Expect the benign one allowed and the other two blocked. It spends router tokens.

steps.title: Edit a rails config
steps.body: On the Config tab edit a file, Check (the candidate is loaded in a network-less container) and Apply (restart, a check that the config is served, rollback on failure). Run Check the rails afterwards.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: The Playground sends a chat through the rails with the server's default config.

faq.q: My edit was refused for removing a rail.
faq.a: Removing rails weakens the safety checks, so a candidate that does it is refused unless it carries the line `# nemo-console: allow-weaken-rails`. Add it only when the weakening is deliberate.

faq.q: Validation passed but the rails still misbehave.
faq.a: The load check does not call the model. Run Check the rails after every edit to see real verdicts.

faq.q: Why can't I edit the Python files?
faq.a: Python in a rails config is code that runs in the server, so it is shown read-only. Change it in the repo.

faq.q: What does restart or stop do?
faq.a: Restart restarts the server only; it refuses requests for about 10 s. Stop is a `docker compose stop` of the three containers: nothing is removed.

faq.q: Are probe prompts stored?
faq.a: No. Events carry names and verdicts only, never prompt text.

evaluator.lead: NVIDIA NeMo Evaluator runs offline benchmark suites (GSM8K, MMLU, ...) against router aliases and reports scores per benchmark and model.

steps.title: Install the wrapper
steps.body: In the lab run `clients/nemo-evaluator/install.sh` and `mint-key.sh`. The Status tab then shows the wrapper, the router, the key file, the suites and the cached datasets.

steps.title: Fetch the datasets once
steps.body: Prefetch is the only step with internet access, so it is done by a human on the host and is not a console action. Name the benchmarks you need.

steps.title: Choose a suite
steps.body: Suites live in `suites.yaml` on the Config tab. It is validated by its own schema and by the wrapper's own check.

steps.title: Run it
steps.body: Actions, Run a suite runs in the background, one at a time, takes minutes and spends router tokens.

steps.title: Read the scores
steps.body: The Status tab shows the scores per benchmark and model; Actions, Show a stored run gives any run's summary.

faq.q: Why is there no prefetch button?
faq.a: Prefetch needs the internet; everything else runs offline. Keeping it a deliberate host step means the console never opens a route out.

faq.q: Is a repeated run just replayed from a cache?
faq.a: No. Every request asks the router to skip its cache, so a repeat is a fresh generation.

faq.q: Which benchmarks can run?
faq.a: Rule-scored ones only: no benchmark that needs a Docker sandbox or an LLM judge.

faq.q: How offline is a run?
faq.a: The wrapper switches the benchmark libraries offline, and a traced full run connected only to loopback. Prefetch is the one step that uses the internet.

faq.q: My run is `interrupted`.
faq.a: The console stopped while it ran. Start it again.

modelopt.lead: NVIDIA Model Optimizer compresses a pinned checkpoint offline (quantization or REAP expert pruning). A job takes a GPU for hours and writes a new checkpoint; it runs in the background and the console reads its verdict, size and compression ratio.

steps.title: Install the wrapper
steps.body: In the lab, `clients/modelopt/install.sh` builds the offline container from checksum-pinned wheels and puts `modelopt-local` on PATH. The container has no network and no Hugging Face token; the model store is mounted read-only, so the base checkpoint must already be there.

steps.title: Write a recipe
steps.body: Recipes live in `recipes.yaml` on the Config tab: `version: 1`, and per recipe a `method` (`reap`, `quantize` or `minitron`), a `base_model` (`org/name`) and an `output` under `/runs/`, with optional `description`, `preset`, `sparsity` and `config`. Unknown keys are refused with their line number.

steps.title: Start a job
steps.body: Actions, Run a compression job is disruptive: it holds a GPU for hours and slows the engines that share it. The wrapper returns at once and the job keeps running after you close the tab.

steps.title: Read the verdict
steps.body: Actions, Show a job gives the verdict, the recipe and the size numbers; the Status tab charts jobs, output size and the ratio to the base.

faq.q: Can I cancel a running job?
faq.a: Not from the console: it only starts jobs and reads verdicts, and the wrapper has no cancel verb. It never stops a running job.

faq.q: A Minitron recipe is refused.
faq.a: Minitron needs Megatron-Core, which the lab's offline container does not ship. The wrapper refuses it with a clear message instead of pretending; it needs NVIDIA's NeMo container.

faq.q: REAP failed on my model.
faq.a: REAP prunes the experts of a mixture-of-experts model; on a dense model it fails. Use `quantize` for dense checkpoints.

faq.q: Does the compression ratio tell me the quality?
faq.a: No. Calibration uses synthetic data in the offline container, so a finished job proves the mechanics, not the quality. Benchmark the result before you serve it.

faq.q: The job would not start: not enough free GPU memory.
faq.a: The wrapper refuses when the freest card has too little free memory, and it never stops an engine for itself. Free a card first, or wait.

faq.q: Why are there no numbers?
faq.a: Every number comes from a finished job's `run.json`; nothing is estimated. With no job yet only the job count (0) is shown.

gym.lead: NVIDIA NeMo Gym runs reinforcement-learning environments and rollouts, contained: each Gym command runs in a client container on an internal network whose only way out is a router broker. A smoke run rolls out a few scored tasks and the console keeps the numbers.

steps.title: Install the wrapper
steps.body: In the lab run `clients/nemo-gym/gym-local build` and `gym-local key` (the pinned image and the wrapper's own router key, local aliases only), and link `gym-local` onto the console's PATH.

steps.title: Check the containment
steps.body: The Status tab shows the wrapper, the broker, the client network, the image and whether the key file is set. Actions, Check the containment confirms against Docker that the client network is internal. Read-only.

steps.title: Run a smoke rollout
steps.body: Actions, Run a smoke rollout takes a model and 1 to 20 tasks. It is disruptive (router tokens on a shared engine), runs in the background and one at a time.

steps.title: Read the rewards
steps.body: Actions, Show a run gives the verdict, model, rollouts and rewards; the Status tab charts runs, mean reward and pass@1.

faq.q: The system is down with `gym.not_contained`.
faq.a: The client network exists but is not internal, so Gym could reach out past the broker. Fix the network in the lab (`clients/nemo-gym`), then run Check the containment again.

faq.q: The broker is stopped. Is that a fault?
faq.a: No. A stopped broker is normal and is not counted as a fault.

faq.q: Why is there no Config tab?
faq.a: The Gym environment config belongs to the lab wrapper, not to the console.

faq.q: Can I train a model on the rollouts here?
faq.a: No. Training (NeMo RL) is not installed, so there is nothing to start or read yet.

faq.q: My run is `interrupted`.
faq.a: The console restarted while it ran. Start it again.

faq.q: Where do the reward numbers come from?
faq.a: From the console's own `run.json` of a finished smoke run, parsed from the wrapper's printed result. Nothing is estimated.

flare.lead: NVIDIA Flare is NVIDIA's research-prototype inference server, written in Rust. It serves a package prepared ahead of time (kernels, CUDA graphs and weights), once per GPU family and tensor-parallel size, on that family. The console runs it on two chip families: sm120 (RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090) and sm121 (one DGX Spark, or several as one engine). It is an experiment lane, off by default; upstream says it is not a replacement for production engines.

steps.title: Link the launcher
steps.body: Every action runs the lab launcher `flare-local`, which is `inference/flare/flare.sh`. Link it onto the console's PATH once; the Status tab then lists every target with its chip, package family, container, image, packages and whether its GPUs are free.

steps.title: Pick a target
steps.body: The launcher defines the targets: each has its hosts, a chip (sm120 takes gb202 packages, sm121 gb10) and the tensor-parallel sizes it can run (for example tp1 and tp2 on two local cards, tp1 on one remote card or one Spark, tp4 across four Sparks). Actions, Show every target prints the table; the action forms offer exactly those names.

steps.title: Prepare a package on that family
steps.body: Ignition prepares a package on the real GPUs of its family, offline, and it needs them to itself for hours. Actions, How to prepare a package prints the sequence for the checkpoints on hand. The lab never downloads the community's ready packages: their licence is not accepted.

steps.title: Stage a remote target
steps.body: A remote host loads the serving image from the console host's share (amd64 or arm64) and gets a trust dir, the io_uring seccomp profile, the public publisher key and the serving key. Create the serving key once on the console host first; it is never printed.

steps.title: Check, then start
steps.body: Check a start runs every precondition and changes nothing. Start Flare refuses unless every GPU of the target is free, and never stops another engine: free the cards yourself. Loading runs in the background (for a multi-host target a peer transfer over the fabric too); then Show the last start.

steps.title: Prove it
steps.body: Probe sends one real completion; /health alone is not proof. The Status tab charts tokens, running requests and draft acceptance per target while it serves; Stop Flare frees the GPUs.

faq.q: Why can a package not run on every target?
faq.a: A package is fixed to a GPU family and a tensor-parallel size when it is prepared: gb202 (RTX PRO 6000 and RTX 5090, sm120) or gb10 (DGX Spark, sm121), and tp1, tp2 or tp4. A tp2 package cannot load as tp1, and an sm120 package fails the architecture check on a Spark. Prepare one per target family on that family's GPUs.

faq.q: Start Flare refuses: a GPU is busy.
faq.a: That is on purpose. The launcher never stops another engine, because whatever holds the GPUs is someone's work. A GPU counts as busy when, on a remote host, a running container has a GPU request (other than Flare's own or the DCGM exporter) or a CUDA process runs on it, and on the console host when a card has more than 3 GiB in use. Stop that engine yourself with its own script, then start Flare.

faq.q: Why is the playground only for the local target?
faq.a: The console's own HTTP stays on loopback, and only the local target listens there. Remote targets serve on the private fabric with a serving key; use Probe for them, which runs through the launcher.

faq.q: Does stopping one Spark touch the multi-Spark engine?
faq.a: No. A single-host engine and a multi-host engine use different container names, and `down` only stops the kind its target names. Starting either refuses while the other runs on that host.

faq.q: Why can I not edit the compose files here?
faq.a: Flare is started only through `flare.sh`, which checks the GPUs first; a bare compose start skips those checks. The files are shown read-only and change in git.

faq.q: The status says the image is not loaded on a remote target.
faq.a: Save the serving image to the console host's share once (`flare-local save-image amd64` for an x86 host; the arm64 image for the Sparks is built on a Spark), then Stage that target. Stage loads the tarball only if its digest matches the one `save-image` kept on the console host, off the share.

faq.q: A target says it could not be checked.
faq.a: Its host did not answer ssh within a few seconds. The page keeps showing the last report and checks again about once a minute; the launcher never waits long on a dead host.
